title: Burst-amortization quant heuristics — lab notes
summary: Working notes from exploratory experiments that probe how short, high-QPS bursts interact with INT8/AWQ/FP8 kernel variants and caching heuristics. Goal: find cheap, low-risk heuristics that reduce p99 tail during bursty traffic without compromising customer-quality budgets.
content:
Purpose:

Quick lab notes capturing the burst-amortization experiments we ran (Sep 7-14 2026) to evaluate quantized kernels under short, high-QPS bursts. This is an exploratory doc — contains raw observations, informal hypotheses, and next-step experiments. Not final recommendations.

Context / motivation:

- Production incidents in Aug/early-Sep showed p99 spikes during 10–30s bursts on Dedicated clusters for a subset of customers. Those customers use pinned INT8/GPTQ models for cost reasons.
- We suspect the combination of kernel switchover, KV-cache pressure, and short-lived batching/shard reassign leads to amplification of latency tails.
- Objective: identify heuristics that "amortize" the cost of switching to cheaper quant kernels during short bursts (i.e., pay a small steady overhead to avoid big p99 spikes) while keeping quality regression within the accepted delta for each customer tier.

What we tested (high level):

1) Kernel variants: 
   - baseline FP16 kernel (serving-runtime/kern-v2.1)
   - INT8-GPTQ kernel (kern-int8-gptq-v3)
   - AWQ-style low-bit path (kern-awq-exp-0.8)
   - experimental FP8 fast-path (kern-fp8-mini-0.3)

2) Heuristics / amortization strategies:
   - Sticky kernel: avoid switching kernels unless burst length > T_threshold (we tried T=5s, 10s, 20s)
   - Pre-warm: proactively sample a small probe (1–2 requests) on cheaper kernel during idle periods so keys/kernels are resident when a burst begins
   - Gradual degrade: route 10% of requests to cheaper kernel during steady-state to keep it warm (randomized)
   - Hybrid batching: temporarily lower max_batch_size to favor latency during bursts but keep continuous small batches to feed cheaper kernels' memory patterns

3) Workloads:
   - Synthetic short prompts (avg tokens 30, tail 150) to emulate chat snippets
   - Long-context summarization (avg tokens 1024) to stress KV cache and different kernel code paths
   - Customer-sim corpus: anonymized support-case dialogues (from infra dataset infra-corp-01)

4) Hardware & infra:
   - Dedicated A100-80GB pool (zone us-west-2-ded-01)
   - Mixed cluster nodes with older Ampere variants to reproduce heterogeneity
   - Serving runtime: main branch commit abc1234; experimental kernel builds from PR 4321

Measurement methodology:

- Burst generator: closed-loop generator that ramps from 50 rps to 1200 rps over 2s, holds for 10s, then decays. 50k requests per run. 10 replicates per config.
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (request-level and token-level), tokens/sec, kernel-switch rate (switches/min), KV cache evictions/min, GPU mem high-water mark, retry/fallback counts, quality delta (ROUGE-1 and a small set of unit prompts with ground-truth logits to compute L2 divergence).
- Logging: high-frequency event logs (10ms granularity) and per-token timing where feasible.

Key observations (raw):

1) Baseline (no amortization): switching to INT8-GPTQ during burst onset produced a 1.9–2.3x increase in request p99 for short prompts (30 tokens) compared to FP16 on the same cluster. The predominant pattern: near-instant kernel switchover at burst start induced scheduler delays and an observed "double-swing" where both kernels fought for dispatcher threads.

2) Sticky kernel (T=10s) reduced p99 spikes by ~45% vs naive switch-on-burst for short bursts but caused ~6% sustained increase in p95 during steady-state for long-context workloads (cache mismatch).

3) Pre-warm probes (one 16-token probe every 15s) significantly reduced kernel-switch overhead; p99 improvement ~30% vs naive switch, with negligible quality delta. However, probe overhead adds ~0.6% additional token cost.

4) Randomized 10% steady routing to cheaper kernel (hybrid) eliminated most cold-switch spikes (p99 down by 55%) but introduced small, systematic regenerative jitter: occasionally a request routed to cheaper kernel hit a rare quant-failure path we saw in 1/4000 requests (reproducible, investigating).

5) FP8 fast-path showed strong throughput improvements but had larger quality variance on long-context summarization (ROUGE-1 drops 0.8–1.2 points vs FP16 on certain prompts). Not acceptable for enterprise customers without fallback.

6) KV cache thrash was a dominant signal for long-context cases: when probes or sticky heuristics failed to align with the active keyset, cache eviction rates rose and latency tails reappeared.

Anomalies & notable incidents:

- Rare 5–10s stall episodes when hybrid routing hit a specific kernel build (kern-awq-exp-0.8@b12). Stack traces point to a mutex contention in dispatcher->kernel-queue when concurrent prefetches occur. Filed INF-7829.
- Memory high-water on older Ampere nodes increased by ~8% when using AWQ path due to an auxiliary scratch buffer; magnified p99 under high-concurrency.

Quality checks:

- Single-token-prompt logits deviance used as a cheap proxy for output quality drift. We added a small prompt set (quality-quickset-12) — across experiments, AWQ-int8 drift remained under per-customer thresholds for 85% of prompts; FP8 failed acceptance on ~20% of cases for long-context tasks.

Hypotheses (informal):

- Kernel switchover overhead ~= dispatcher contention + cold kernel warmup (JIT/kernels + cache permissions). So amortization reduces frequency of the high-cost event.
- Warmup probes work because they reduce the probability of a cold kernel path being the first work a GPU sees after idle; they effectively prime allocator/cache.
- Randomized steady routing keeps cheaper kernel state warm at low steady cost but increases attack surface for kernel-specific rare failures.

Action items / next experiments:

1) Instrumentation: add per-kernel queueing metrics and allocator hit-rate counters. (Owner: Jared, ticket INF-7894)
2) Run a controlled study varying probe cadence (every 5s / 15s / 30s) and probe size (8/16/32 tokens) to find knee for cost vs p99 improvement. (Owner: Priya)
3) Reproduce mutex contention locally with stress harness that interleaves pre-warm and burst routing to AWQ build b12; gather flamegraphs. Try simple backoff at dispatcher level. (Owner: Erik, linked INF-7829)
4) Evaluate hybrid routing with a safety net: if kernel-specific error observed, circuit-breaker trips that routes 100% to FP16 for 60s and logs sample traces (Goal: avoid cascading tail events). Implement feature flag. (Owner: Aparna)
4b) Add small quality regression test to automated rollout to block hybrid routing flag if fail rate > 0.5% on quickset.

5) Cost analysis: compute token-cost delta for pre-warm probes and hybrid 10% routing to estimate break-even per customer tier. Early estimate: pre-warm probes cost ~0.6% tokens, hybrid 10% routing costs ~8–12% token overhead depending on kernel speed differential.

Notes to self / informal thoughts:

- This feels like a "keep-warm" vs "on-demand" problem at many layers: kernel binary + allocator + KV cache + scheduler. Best short-term win seems to be cheap probes combined with sticky thresholding (T~8–12s) and a simple circuit-breaker.
- Need to align with product: for Hosted API we can be more aggressive (tolerate slightly higher drift in edge cases) than Dedicated/Private where customers expect pinning and predictable quality.

References and artifacts:

- PR with AWQ kernels: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4321
- Repro ticket for mutex stall: JIRA INF-7829
- Run logs (s3): s3://redwood-lab/runs/burst-amortization/2026-09-09/ (archived)

Open questions (short):

- Where to expose these heuristics in config? Per-model or per-customer? Lean: per-customer policy with safe defaults.
- Can we build a tiny safety harness that samples outputs from cheaper kernels and auto-rolls them back when regression detected? Feels feasible but needs latency-friendly eval pipeline.

Appendix (quick run notes):

- Command used to start burst harness: ./tools/burst-run --model llm-13b-ctx1024 --kernel=auto --ramp=2s --hold=10s --reps=10 --probe-cadence=15s
- Kernel builds used: kern-int8-gptq-v3@b7, kern-awq-exp-0.8@b12, kern-fp8-mini-0.3@b4
- Quick quality set: quality-quickset-12 (12 prompts, mixed-length)

If you're reading this and want to try something immediately: enable pre-warm probes (fflag: quant_probes=true) on a non-prod pool and run the harness with --probe-size=16 --probe-cadence=15s. Observe p99 on short prompt runs.

— Aparna
